opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated levers you have, honestly. When you're early in your career, there's this instinct that your impact is basically the code you write or the experiments you run yourself. But in a big organization working on something like large-scale model training, the bottleneck is very often not raw technical ability. It's that someone brilliant is stuck waiting on compute allocation, or they don't know who owns a particular piece of infrastructure, or there's some decision that needs to get made and nobody feels empowered to make it.

If you can be the person who notices that and just clears the path, whether that's going and talking to the right person, writing the doc that gets everyone aligned, or fixing the annoying tooling issue that everyone's been routing around, you're effectively multiplying the output of a lot of really talented people. A single unblock might save five researchers a week each. That's way more leverage than almost anything I could do sitting alone at my desk.

There's also a compounding effect. When people see that you care about their problems actually getting solved, they come to you earlier, they share context more freely, and you end up with a much better map of where the real bottlenecks in the organization are. That map is incredibly valuable, because it tells you where to point your own technical effort too.

And I'd say it's a bit of an agency thing. A lot of organizational blockers persist simply because everyone assumes someone else is responsible. Being willing to just take ownership, even of things that aren't technically your job, is surprisingly rare, and it ends up mattering a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says Sholto’s impact comes from clearing colleagues’ blockers and multiplying their output, but it does not describe him initiating a direction and mobilizing others around it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated levers in a research org, honestly. When I joined Google, one of the things I noticed pretty quickly was that the limiting factor for a lot of people wasn't intelligence or ideas, it was that they'd hit some wall. They needed compute allocated, or they needed a code review from a team that wasn't prioritizing them, or they didn't know who owned some piece of infrastructure, and they'd just stall. Sometimes for weeks.

And the thing is, a lot of those blockers are trivially solvable if you know the right person or you're willing to be a bit annoying on someone's behalf. So I started spending maybe a chunk of my week just going around asking people, what are you stuck on? And then trying to unstick it. Pinging the person who owned the thing, writing the one-pager that made the ask legible to the people controlling the resource, or sometimes just saying, hey, you're actually allowed to do this, nobody's going to stop you.

The reason it scales is that your own output is bounded by how many hours you can work. But if you can turn five or six people from blocked to unblocked, and each of them is running experiments that matter, that's way more research velocity than you'd ever generate alone. It's also a lot of the reason I think agency is such an important trait in researchers. Most of the time, the permission you're waiting for doesn't exist. You just have to go do it, and then help other people realize they can too.

The other piece is that it compounds. Once people know you're the person who will actually help, they come to you earlier, before they've lost two weeks. And you start to build this map of where the friction is in the organization, which is itself incredibly valuable information. You end up seeing the structural problems that no individual contributor would see from their own corner.

r001.rationale: The response says his impact scales by unblocking colleagues and helping them act, but does not say he mobilizes them around a direction he initiates.

astra-6.text:
I think it can be a huge multiplier. If you make yourself 20 percent more productive, that’s useful. But if you notice that five people are all stuck on the same thing, and you spend an afternoon fixing it, you might have saved weeks of work across the team.

Often the blocker is surprisingly mundane. Someone doesn’t know who owns a system, or two teams have different assumptions about what needs to happen next. You can help just by getting the right people into a conversation and making the next step clear.

The thing to watch is whether you’re actually removing the blocker or becoming the person everyone has to go through. Ideally, you leave behind a better tool, clearer ownership, or enough shared context that people can solve the next problem themselves. That’s where the impact really starts to compound.

r001.rationale: The response describes removing shared blockers and coordinating colleagues, but does not say that Sholto initiates a direction and mobilizes others around it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s one of the highest-leverage things you can do. If somebody’s already really capable and motivated, often they don’t need you to help them do the work. They need a decision, or access to some resource, or two teams to agree on who owns something. If you can resolve that, you’ve potentially saved them weeks with an hour of your time.

And that compounds if you fix the underlying problem. You don’t just unblock one person; you make it easier for everyone who comes along afterward. The thing to be careful about is becoming the person every decision has to go through. Ideally, you’re giving people enough context and authority that they can solve the next one themselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes unblocking capable colleagues and fixing organizational obstacles, but does not say Sholto mobilizes others around a direction he initiates.
